Laem Sor Pagoda (Wat Phra Chedi Laem Sor) is a gold-tiled chedi standing right on the shore at the end of Bang Kao beach, on Koh Samui's quiet south coast. Entry is free, the temple is open 07:00–18:00, and a visit takes 30–45 minutes. A white chedi, Khao Chedi, stands on the hill to the west. Come in the late afternoon for the warmest light, and pair it with a Pig Island boat from Thong Krut, a few minutes' drive away.

Map and directions

Laem Sor is on the south coast between Bang Kao and Thong Krut. From the ring road, take Route 4170 towards the south coast and follow the signs for Ban Bang Kao; just past the village, a smaller road leads down to the beach and the temple. The walk from the parking area to the chedi is short and flat.

Get directions: open Laem Sor Pagoda in Google Maps. Some maps label the hill temple as Wat Khao Chedi; it lies a few hundred metres west.

History of Laem Sor Pagoda

The site is far older than the shining tiles suggest. Temple history records that the first chedi here was built around 1907 under Phra Khru Wiboon Thammasan (also known as Phet Tisso), then head of the island's monks. It stood on a small hill and was built not of fired brick but of blocks of coral stone, bound with natural materials; villagers from around Samui carried the building materials up from the shore. Buddha relics, said to have come from Sri Lanka, were enshrined inside.

In 1967 lightning struck and damaged the top of the hilltop chedi. A new chedi was then built on the shore below, and the relics were moved into it. That seaside chedi, covered in yellow-glazed tiles that shine gold in the sun, is the one most visitors photograph today. The older hilltop chedi was restored by Thailand's Fine Arts Department in 2004, and the site was formally registered as a temple, Wat Phra Chedi Laem Sor, in 2011, although monks and villagers had worshipped here for over a century.

The monk credited with building the seaside chedi is remembered locally as Luang Pho Daeng. He is a different person from the mummified Luang Pho Daeng at Wat Khunaram, although both were Samui monks of the same era.

What you'll see, step by step

  1. 1. The guardians. Two large, brightly painted yak (giant) guardians with swords stand at the entrance. Behind them is a small shrine hall with a golden Buddha image; take your shoes off before stepping in.
  2. 2. The chedi. The gold-tiled chedi stands on a low rocky outcrop at sea level, with the Gulf of Thailand behind it. Walk around it clockwise. On a clear day you can see the small islands off the south-west coast, including Koh Tan and Koh Madsum (Pig Island).
  3. 3. The boat-shaped hall. About 100 m away is a hall shaped like a ship, with a figure of the monk who built the chedi. Locals pray here, and when a wish comes true some leave a small model boat as thanks.
  4. 4. The grounds. Beyond the chedi are a small forest, a pond, tables and benches. It is a quiet place to sit; there is little shade at the chedi itself.
  5. 5. Khao Chedi (optional). The white chedi on the hill to the west. See the next section.

Khao Chedi: the hilltop chedi

A white chedi stands on the hill a few hundred metres west of Laem Sor, in a temple that maps label as Wat Khao Chedi. The climb takes some effort in the heat, but the view over the south coast and the islands towards Koh Tan is one of the best on this side of Samui, and you will rarely share it with more than a handful of people. Wear proper shoes, take water, and avoid the climb in the middle of the day. Whether this white chedi is the original 1907 coral-stone chedi restored in 2004 is something we are confirming with the temple. [check]

Laem Sor etiquette and dress code

  • Cover shoulders and knees. People come straight from the beach here, but beachwear is not appropriate at the chedi or in the halls. Bring a sarong.
  • Shoes off inside the shrine hall; sandals are fine around the chedi. The tiles and stone get very hot by midday.
  • Walk clockwise around the chedi and don't climb on it or its base for photos.
  • Swimming: the beach is shallow and rocky in front of the chedi; swim elsewhere and don't change clothes in the temple grounds.
  • Buddhist holy days bring many local worshippers; visit quietly and give way to people praying.
  • Women should not touch monks or hand them items directly.

Best time and light

The late afternoon (about 16:00–18:00) gives the warmest light on the gold tiles and the calmest feel. Mornings are cooler and also quiet. Because there is no coach park, Laem Sor is rarely crowded at any time of day, a big contrast with Big Buddha. By season: February to April is the driest and calmest; October to December is the north-east monsoon, with November the wettest month (about 445 mm). The south coast is somewhat sheltered from north-east swell, but heavy rain still comes in sudden bursts and the stone is slippery when wet.

Parking, facilities and accessibility

  • Parking: a small parking area by the temple; big tour buses don't come here.
  • Facilities: limited; a visitor centre, basic toilets and little else. Bring water and sun protection.
  • Accessibility: the path from the parking area to the chedi is flat and easy, suitable for most visitors including those with pushchairs; the outcrop is uneven at the edges. Khao Chedi is a climb and not suitable for wheelchairs.
  • Food: local restaurants in Bang Kao village and seafood places towards Thong Krut.

There is no bus or regular songthaew to the temple itself, so come by scooter, car, Grab or taxi. Grab cars are scarce in the south; for the return, ask your driver to wait or arrange a pickup. Taxis don't use meters, so agree the fare first. Route 4170 has steep, narrow sections that are slippery when wet; ride slowly and wear a helmet (fine up to 2,000 THB). See getting around Koh Samui and Koh Samui roads.

Seasonal and safety notes

  • Heat: the chedi stands in full sun on bare rock. From March to May, highs reach 32–33 °C and the tiles burn bare feet; go before 10:00 or after 16:00.
  • Rain: in the north-east monsoon (October to December) showers are heavy and sudden. Wet tiles and coral stone are slippery, and Route 4170's steep sections need care on a scooter.
  • Waves: keep off the outer rocks of the outcrop when the sea is up, especially with children.
  • Jellyfish: if you swim nearby, use the vinegar stations at hotels and see our beach safety guide. Emergency numbers: ambulance 1669, Tourist Police 1155.

Add a Pig Island boat from Thong Krut

Thong Krut, the pier for Pig Island, is the closest departure point to Laem Sor. Pig Island trips run every day of the year. Ang Thong Marine Park is closed from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December.
